questions.solution:
Metals typically have the following characteristic properties:

· Lustrous (shiny) appearance

· Good conductors of heat and electricity

· Malleable and ductile (not brittle)

· Tend to lose electrons and form cations in solution, not anions

questions.solution:
Statement I is correct; Metal oxides (e.g., Na₂O, CaO) are usually basic (react with acids to form salt + water). Some (like Al₂O₃) are amphoteric.

Statement II is incorrect; Most nonmetals are poor conductors (except graphite/carbon). They lack free electrons for conduction.

Statement III is correct; Metalloids (e.g., Si, Ge) show mixed properties (semiconductors, brittle but shiny).

Metallic oxides are generally basic and ionic and often dissolve in water to form metal hydroxides.

Basic Nature:

o Most metallic oxides react with acids to form salt and water, exhibiting basic behavior.

o Example:

Na2O+H2SO4→Na2SO4+H2O

Ionic Character:

o Metallic oxides are typically ionic compounds (composed of metal cations Mn+and oxide anions O2-)

o This is due to the large electronegativity difference between metals and oxygen.

Exceptions:

· Some metallic oxides (e.g., Al2O3, ZnO) are amphoteric (can act as both acidic and basic).

· Transition metal oxides (e.g., Mn2O7​) can be acidic, but these are exceptions rather than the rule.

As you move from left to right across a period in the periodic table:

· Atomic size decreases

· Effective nuclear charge increases

· Tendency to lose electrons (metallic character) decreases

This is because elements on the left side (like alkali metals) easily lose electrons and are highly metallic, whereas elements on the right side (like nonmetals) gain electrons and show non-metallic character.

Metalloids have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals. They can act as semiconductors under the right conditions, are solid at room temperature, and can form amphoteric oxides.

Silicon is a metalloid, meaning it has properties that are intermediate between metals and nonmetals.

At room temperature (around 25°C):

· Bromine (Br₂) is a reddish-brown liquid, and it's the only non-metal that exists as a liquid under standard conditions.

· Oxygen (O₂) and nitrogen (N₂) are gases at room temperature.

· Carbon exists as a solid (like graphite or diamond).

· Metals have a tendency to lose electrons during chemical reactions.

· This results in the formation of positively charged ions, called cations.

· This behavior is due to their low ionization energies and the desire to attain a stable noble gas configuration.

questions.solution:
For Alkali Metals (Group 1), the ionization energy decreases as you move down the group. Metals are electropositive elements with relatively low ionization energies, meaning they easily lose electrons. Ionization energy generally decreases down a group for metals and increases across a period.

For Halogens (Group 17), the electronegativity generally decreases down the group (though this is not explicitly stated as a trend in this section, the increasing atomic radius and shielding effect would imply this).

For Nonmetals in general (considering Group trends), the metallic character decreases as you move up a group (implying nonmetallic character increases).

· Down any group:

o Atomic radius increases

o Ionization energy decreases

o Metallic character increases (for metals)

o Electronegativity decreases (for nonmetals)

· Non-metals generally form acidic oxides (like CO₂, SO₂, NO₂), which react with water to form acids or with bases to form salts.

· Some non-metals (like carbon monoxide, CO or nitric oxide, NO) form neutral oxides, which do not react significantly with acids or bases.

Within any group of elements, the metallic character increases from top to bottom due to decreasing electronegativity and ionization energy.

As you move from top to bottom in a group of the periodic table:

· Atomic size increases

· Ionization energy decreases

· Electrons are more easily lost, which means metallic character increases

This is why alkali metals like lithium (Li) at the top are less metallic than cesium (Cs) or francium (Fr) at the bottom.

Non-metals are typically brittle, poor conductors of heat and electricity (except graphite), and non-lustrous. Malleability is a characteristic of metals.

· Alkali metals (Group 1 elements like lithium, sodium, potassium, etc.) have one electron in their outermost shell.

· They readily lose that one electron to achieve a stable noble gas configuration.

· As a result, they form ions with a +1 charge → M → M⁺ + e⁻

The transition of the valence electron of sodium results in the release of a photon with a wavelength of 589 nm, which appears yellow in a flame test.

· Lithium (Li) → Crimson red flame

· Potassium (K) → Lilac/pale violet flame

· Rubidium (Rb) → Red-violet flame

Alkaline earth metals (Group 2 elements like magnesium, calcium, etc.) are generally:

· Harder than alkali metals (Group 1 like sodium, potassium).

· Less reactive than alkali metals.

· More dense than alkali metals.

· Not softer - alkali metals are very soft and can often be cut with a knife.

The diatomic halogen fluorine is described as a pale yellow gas.

· Chlorine (Cl₂) is a greenish-yellow gas.

· Bromine (Br₂) is a reddish-brown liquid.

· Iodine (I₂) is a dark violet solid that sublimates to a violet vapor.

Oxygen is one of the seven non-metals that exist under standard conditions as diatomic molecules (O₂).

· Oxygen (O₂) exists as a diatomic molecule under standard conditions (O=O).

· Several non-metals like hydrogen (H₂), nitrogen (N₂), fluorine (F₂), chlorine (Cl₂), bromine (Br₂), iodine (I₂) also exist as diatomic molecules.

· Sulfur typically exists as S₈ (a puckered ring structure).

· Carbon exists as solid forms like graphite or diamond.

· Boron is a solid metalloid under standard conditions.

Group 16 elements (also known as the oxygen family or chalcogens) include:

· Oxygen (O)

· Sulfur (S)

· Selenium (Se)

· Tellurium (Te)

· Polonium (Po)

As you move down the group:

· Atomic size increases

· Ionization energy decreases

· The tendency to lose electrons increases → more metallic behavior

Magnesium is a metal, and like most metals:

· It is a good conductor of electricity

· It forms basic oxides (e.g., MgO, which reacts with acids to form salt and water)

Why the others are incorrect:

· Sulfur - Non-metal; poor conductor and forms acidic oxides

· Chlorine - Non-metal; gas at room temperature, forms acidic oxides

· Phosphorus - Non-metal; forms acidic oxides like P₂O₅

questions.solution:
I. They have low ionization energies is Correct - Alkali metals (Group 1) have a single electron in their outermost shell, which is easily lost. Hence, they have low ionization energies.

II. Their reactivity decreases as you move down the group is Incorrect - Reactivity increases as you go down the group due to increasing atomic size and decreasing ionization energy.

III. They are found in nature in their elemental form is incorrect - Alkali metals are highly reactive and are not found in nature in their elemental form. They are usually found as compounds (e.g., NaCl, K₂CO₃).

questions.solution:
Halogens (Group 17 elements: Fluorine, Chlorine, Bromine, Iodine, Astatine) are non-metals, except astatine, which is a metalloid or weakly metallic. So this statement I is false.

Statement II is correct. Halogens readily gain electrons to achieve a noble gas configuration, which means they have very high electron affinities. In fact, chlorine has one of the highest electron affinity values among all elements.
